category.text: $course$/Game Theory/Chapter 07 - Repeated Games, Reciprocity and the Folk Theorem (Quiz)

questiontext.text: The Prisoner's Dilemma is repeated exactly 20 times and both players know it. What is the unique subgame perfect equilibrium?

generalfeedback.text: Backward induction from round 20: with no future, both defect. That makes round 19 effectively terminal, and so on to round 1. Defection in every round is the unique SPNE. What matters is the known last round, not the finiteness of expected play.

answer.text: Both players defect in every round
Both cooperate until round 19, then defect

feedback.text: Round 19 unravels for the same reason as round 20.
There is no future to protect in the last round.

questiontext.text: A player receives a payoff of 6 every period forever, with discount factor \(\delta = 0.75\). What is the present value of this stream?

generalfeedback.text: The geometric sum gives \(\dfrac{6}{1 - 0.75} = \dfrac{6}{0.25} = 24\). This formula is the workhorse of every repeated-game computation.

questiontext.text: In a Prisoner's Dilemma with \(T = 5\), \(R = 3\), \(P = 1\), \(S = 0\), what is the smallest discount factor \(\delta\) for which grim trigger sustains cooperation? Give a decimal.
Axelrod credited tit-for-tat's tournament success to four properties. Which property does grim trigger lack?

generalfeedback.text: Grim trigger is nice, retaliatory and clear, but never forgiving: one defection - even an accidental one - condemns the relationship to permanent punishment. In noisy environments this makes grim trigger far worse than tit-for-tat or tit-for-two-tats.

feedback.text: It is very easy to describe and predict.

questiontext.text: Tit-for-tat is a dominant strategy in the infinitely repeated Prisoner's Dilemma.

generalfeedback.text: False. Against a player who always defects, tit-for-tat loses the first round and only matches thereafter, so Always Defect would have done better. Tit-for-tat performs well in populations of reciprocators, which is a statement about environments, not dominance.

questiontext.text: The folk theorem for infinitely repeated games says that, for players patient enough:

generalfeedback.text: Any feasible payoff vector strictly above every player's minmax level can be supported as a subgame perfect equilibrium. The result explains how norms and reputations become self-enforcing, but it also means the theory has very little predictive bite without further restrictions.

answer.text: Essentially any feasible payoff vector above the minmax can be supported as a subgame perfect equilibrium
Only the efficient outcome can be supported
Only the stage-game Nash equilibrium can be supported
Cooperation is impossible without an external enforcer

name.text: C07 Q7 - What restores cooperation in finite games

questiontext.text: Introducing a small probability that one player is a committed cooperator can restore long stretches of cooperation in a finitely repeated Prisoner's Dilemma.

generalfeedback.text: True. Kreps, Milgrom, Roberts and Wilson (1982) showed that a little incomplete information about types gives rational players an incentive to build a reputation for cooperating, sustaining cooperation until near the end. This is the bridge to Chapter 8.

questiontext.text: Same Prisoner's Dilemma but the temptation payoff rises to T = 7 (still R = 3, P = 1, S = 0). What is the new critical discount factor for grim trigger? Give a decimal to two places.

generalfeedback.text: \(\delta^{*} = \dfrac{T-R}{T-P} = \dfrac{7-3}{7-1} = \dfrac{2}{3} \approx 0.67\). A bigger prize for cheating requires more patience to keep cooperation alive.
